doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Army service: K.P., the Eighth Armored Division and the camp band
summary: Gibbs describes boot camp punishment, being made a tank driver, then being put in an Army band in Dallas on drums and vibes, never rising above corporal.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: He really could. Let me go back a little bit. You did some service in World War II.
What kind of service did you do?
Well it’s wild. They don’t tell you in the Army what you’re going to do. Want me to tell you my first experiences in the Army?

I was very young and I couldn’t talk, I used to box. I wanted to be a fighter. And there was one, you know when you first go in they send you to I think Fort Dix, the big camp where before they send you out to wherever you’re going to go, they get thousands of guys there and all you do is walk around picking up cigarette butts. They have to kill time until they find a place where you’re going to go. Well 39 years old I think was the age where you got dis— you couldn’t get in the Army after 39. And I was 18. And this one guy was a PFC, kept picking on this guy who at that time I thought was an old guy, because I was 18 and he was 39. I thought he was old. Now he could be my grandson. I thought he was old. And so he kept picking at him. And so I said, “Hey listen, why don’t you give the rest of us something to do, you know, he’s an older guy here.” He takes me out and he says, “What’s your name?” I thought he was going to make me a sergeant, what do you mean. So I told him Private Julius Gubenko.” He says, “What barracks?” He took down the name. General the next day, you know. Four o’clock in the morning, that guy came in, “Gubenko?” I said, “Yeah.” “You’re on K.P.” He said, “I know you have to do that,” and you serve thousands of guys. And then whenever you serve them then you go home usually. “Gubenko, you guys stay and you have to clean out the pots and pans.” I’m talking about funky pots and pans. So I did that and I went back to bed about two o’clock in the morning. Four o’clock in the morning, again, the same guy woke me up for K.P. and I went through the same thing. And the next night he did it again. And now I knew what he was doing, because of what I did and I said, “Listen, why don’t we go outside and fight and get this over with?” No fighting, you do K.P. He wouldn’t fight me and he had me do K.P. for five days until I didn’t say a word. I mean it taught me something. I finally got shipped out, but I was done. K.P., you name it. But then I got into — guys who were about 24 years old were in bands. At 18 you were a baby and they

were much older to me too. I went into the Eighth Armored Division as a tank driver. And you know, like I say, in the Army they don’t tell you what you’re going to do. So I was a tank driver, I was driving a tank. Then they put me in the band. They put me in the band because they needed — nobody played vibes. I wanted to play drums so bad, really, but they didn’t have vibes so they put me in the band. Now the infiltration course is where they have barbed wire about this high and you have to crawl underneath through mud with the thing exploding. And this is World War II where there is no games. We had to beat Hitler and his gang, where they actually shot real bullets overhead, real bullets. Because if you sit up you can get hurt, killed, but if you did it overseas you can kill everybody else because — so that was the training. So I did that and I was ready to go overseas and they don’t tell you, Private Gubenko, once again, they ship me to Dallas, Texas, they put together a band to make music, the Army picks it. And they need a percussion player. So I would be up playing drums in the band, which I wanted to do, with 30 strings and all, a big thing, and I’d play some vibes once in a while too, because they had a bunch of drummers. And I wound up writing a lot of arrangements, doing the whole thing. Never could get a rating, because also in those days we used to listen to Woody Herman’s band on the radio and Davy Tough was playing drums and when Davy would finish the song it would be cut off and he goes [scats] he did some extra beats. So every time in the band, boy I was hip you know. He’d cut us off and I’d go [scats]. He says, “Hey what are you doing, I gave you a cut off.” I says, “Yeah, but Davy Tough.” He says, “I don’t care about Davy Tough or Woody Herman. And I never could get — when I got discharged, like eighty years later, I was finally a corporal. I finally kept my mouth shut. If you’re not the band leader, don’t say anything. But it took a while.
I have a feeling you still have to get the last word in.
